analysis.one_liner: Raises the bar for civil asset forfeiture and stops police from keeping seized property.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after bipartisan introduction with 28 cosponsors, it sat in four House committees for 21 months and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal and state police can seize a person's cash, car, or home on suspicion it is connected to a crime, even when no one is ever convicted. The owner then has to fight in court to get it back, and under current law the government only has to prove its case at the lowest legal standard, while the seized money helps pay for the same police work. This bill would raise the government's proof standard to 'clear and convincing evidence,' guarantee owners a lawyer, require the owner to have knowingly been involved in the crime, and send all forfeiture proceeds to the general Treasury instead of law enforcement accounts. It would also end 'equitable sharing,' the program that passes federal forfeiture money to state and local police.
analysis.who_benefits: Property owners — including people never charged with any crime — whose cash, vehicles, or homes are seized under civil forfeiture. They would get an attorney, a 14-day probable-cause hearing for seized bank accounts, a higher proof standard, and a court weighing whether taking the property is excessive compared to the offense. Taxpayers generally also benefit, because seizure proceeds would go to the Treasury rather than feeding a self-funding enforcement cycle.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People whose property police seize without a conviction

how_it_helps.text: Requires the government to prove a forfeiture case by clear and convincing evidence instead of a mere preponderance, and to prove the owner knowingly used or consented to the property's use in the offense [S2] [S3].
Guarantees the right to counsel in all civil forfeiture proceedings [S2].

Directs proceeds from seized property into the Treasury's General Fund instead of Department of Justice accounts, ending the arrangement in which the agency doing the seizing keeps the money [S2] [S3].

Eliminates equitable sharing payments that route federally forfeited property to state and local police, a channel that has let local departments collect federal proceeds their own state laws restrict [S2].

Adds a knowing-intent requirement to structuring prosecutions and requires a probable-cause hearing within 14 days after cash is seized in a structuring case, with the money returned if no probable cause is found [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies, chiefly the Department of Justice and state and local police departments, which would lose the forfeiture revenue and equitable-sharing payments they now use to fund operations, vehicles, and equipment outside the normal appropriations process.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal and state law enforcement agencies

drawbacks.text: Prosecutors and police argue the higher proof standard and owner-fault requirement would make it harder to strip drug trafficking organizations of their illicit proceeds, since civil forfeiture is one of the few tools that works when a low-level courier, not a cartel boss, holds the cash.

Ending equitable sharing and Treasury deposit means law enforcement loses hundreds of millions of dollars in self-generated revenue; opponents contend this defunds anti-drug operations, while supporters see exactly that self-funding as the conflict of interest the bill is designed to fix [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is between property rights and police revenue. The protections address a well-documented problem: seizure without conviction under a low proof standard, with proceeds flowing back to the seizing agency. Clear-and-convincing evidence still allows genuine forfeiture of criminal proceeds, so the bill does not abolish the tool — it removes the financial incentive and raises the burden. The main cost is less forfeiture-funded enforcement, which Congress could replace through appropriations if it chose. On balance the safeguards outweigh the funding loss.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees and then to two subcommittees, no committee ever took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Tim Walberg (R-MI) introduced the bill on March 27, 2019, with five original cosponsors from both parties: Jamie Raskin (D-MD), Thomas Massie (R-KY), Tony Cárdenas (D-CA), Tom McClintock (R-CA), and Bobby Rush (D-IL) [S1] [S3].
It drew 28 cosponsors by the end of the Congress, split evenly between 14 of 231 House Democrats and 14 of 197 House Republicans [S4].

The Speaker referred it to four committees — Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Financial Services — splitting it among panels with different priorities, a common routing that makes action harder [S5].

It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, and no committee reported it, no markup was held, and no floor vote ever occurred [S5].
The bill died at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021, and all its work lapsed [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal law enforcement agencies and state and local police departments, which kept the existing system in which they seize property, meet a low proof standard, and keep the proceeds. Property owners remained subject to the same seizure rules the bill would have changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies that keep seizure proceeds

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement agencies (DOJ, DEA, FBI)
industries.note: The bill would send forfeiture proceeds to the Treasury instead of DOJ's own accounts, ending a revenue stream that funds enforcement operations from property taken from the public. Their funding interest runs directly against the property rights of the people they seize from.

Eliminating equitable sharing ends the flow of federal forfeiture money to local departments, which has been used to reach proceeds that state laws restrict. Local budgets built on seized cash would shrink.

industries.industry: Owners of seized property and civil liberties advocates
industries.note: Property owners, including people never charged with a crime, would gain counsel, a prompt hearing for seized bank accounts, and a higher government burden of proof. Their interest runs with the public's.
